en: The Avadāna on the Benefits of Observing the Vow of Day and Night and Serving the Caityas.
Oṃ, homage to the Triple Gem!
Having bowed to the glorious Triple Gem, the sovereign of the worlds of the three realms,
I shall relate the narrative of the Ahorātra vow according to the instruction of my guru.
With palms joined in reverence, Aśoka respectfully requested Upagupta, the lord of ascetics, as he sat in the Kukkuṭārāma monastery: Avc_2 //

Then King Aśoka, having bowed with palms joined in reverence to the ascetic Upagupta, made this request with great devotion: {A different verse in BCDE as follows: athāśoko mahīpāla upaguptaṃ yatiṃ ca tam / kṛtāñjalipuṭo natvā prārthayad evam ādarāt // Avc_2* //}
"O Venerable One, O True Teacher, I wish to hear once more the ritual for the vow of the shrine (caityavrata), as well as the ritual for the day-and-night vow (ahorātravrata) and its merits. (Avc 3)
Therefore, may you, the true guru and teacher, for the sake of increasing the merit of the world,
deign to instruct us here in the ritual procedure for the day-and-night vow (ahorātravrata).
Having heard this request made by that lord of men, the wise ascetic looked at the king and instructed him once more as follows.
Listen well, O Great King, to that which was spoken by my teacher; I shall declare it to you, and having heard it, act accordingly. (Avc 6)
In the past, that Blessed One, the Teacher, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Guru of the World, was together with his disciples— the monks as well as the novices and lay followers.
Together with nuns of excellent conduct and also with hosts of bodhisattvas, he dwelt in the monastery at Jeta’s Grove, the hermitage of the Sugata.
Then that Blessed One, the Buddha, seated in the midst of the assembly for the sake of increasing the merit of the worlds, began to teach the Dharma.
Then all the world-protectors, such as the Lord of the Immortals and others of great supernatural power,
arrived with faith to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
Brahmā and the other brahmins, as well as the great seers and ascetics,
and the four great kings together with their armies and attendants— Avc_11.
The lords of the Daityas, the kings of the Nāgas, the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras;
the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Sādhyas, the Grahas, and likewise the Vasus.
The great heroic rākṣasas, the garuḍas, and the mahoragas;
the yogins and ascetics, as well as kings and kṣatriyas. Avc_13 //
Ministers and counselors, Vaiśyas and princes, guild-leaders and wealthy men, Śūdras, caravan leaders, and great merchants.
Merchants and artisans, as well as city-dwellers and country-folk, villagers and those from market towns, and likewise inhabitants of other lands.
Having all approached that Buddha Śrīghana with joy, they honored him with faith, worshipped him, and even performed circumambulations. (Avc 16)
Having bowed with palms joined in reverence and gazing [at him], they were filled with great joy;
with concentrated minds, they stood ready to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
Then the elder monk Subhūti, rising from his seat,
adjusted his upper robe and knelt upon the ground with both knees.
Having bowed with palms joined in reverence to the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World, and gazing upon that Śrīghana, he made this request with great devotion: (Avc 19)
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, may you, our Guru, take note:
all these people in the world are gathered here, poised to hear the Dharma from the Teacher.
Therefore, O Lord, tell me when this world-renowned vow of day and night (ahorātravrata) commences here, and explain its ritual procedure. (Avc 21)
When he, the Arhat, had thus questioned him, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages,
looked toward that assembly and Subhūti, and spoke as follows:
Excellent! Listen, Subhūti, you who bear the welfare of all sentient beings;
I shall now describe the meritorious vow for a day and night, along with its ritual procedure.
Long ago, in Pūrvavideha, there was a famous city named Gandhavatī;
in that city, the sovereign lord known as Indradṛṣṭa was a king of great wisdom.
Having brought Vasubandhu, the son of the Conqueror, into the inner apartments,
he placed him upon his own seat in the assembly hall and, having honored him, worshipped him with faith.
Then that king, the lord of the earth, having risen and approached him, bowed with palms joined in reverence and requested this with great respect: Avc_26 //
Venerable One, since these worlds are conceited regarding false dharmas,
please teach the true Dharma in order to destroy their pride.
Upon hearing this, may all these beings be awakened to the true Dharma,
be completely liberated from all evil, and attain enlightenment.
Having heard what was thus requested by the king, Vasubandhu, who knew himself, looked toward that lord of the earth whom Indra had questioned and spoke as follows: Avc_29 //
Listen well, O Great King, for the increase of your merit and for the benefit of all sentient beings: that great vow of day and night. (Avc 30)
Just as I previously heard it proclaimed by Vipaśyin,
the great merit and its benefits, as well as the ritual procedure for it, shall now be explained.
Those men who desire to attain great merit in this saṃsāra should,
with faith and joy, observe the vow of the day and night.
Those mortals who joyfully observe the vow of day and night with devotion—
all of them possess stainless souls and have purified the three spheres.
Having attained the thought of awakening and practiced the conduct of awakening,
one brings about the welfare of all sentient beings and fulfills the perfections in due order.
Having conquered the entire host of afflictions as well as all the hosts of Māras,
and having attained perfect awakening, they will certainly become Sugatas.
Indeed, by all the Victors of the past having undertaken this supreme vow,
they conquered the entire host of Māras and attained perfect awakening.
All the perfectly awakened ones of the present have observed this vow;
indeed, by the power of this merit, they have swiftly attained perfect awakening.
Likewise, having undertaken this excellent vow together with all those of the future,
they shall attain supreme enlightenment through the ripening of this merit.
Likewise, other bodhisattvas who practice the vow for perfect enlightenment,
having taken up this supreme vow, conduct themselves in the discipline of awakening.
Likewise, all the lords of the immortals, having joyfully observed this vow,
become sovereigns of the divine realms and partakers of enlightenment.
In this way, all great beings, as well as seers and sages,
having undertaken this supreme vow, become practitioners of the holy life.
In this way, whatever men joyfully practice this vow,
they all, by virtue of that merit, become partakers of enlightenment.
And those who, having seen or even heard of this vow, rejoice in it—
they too become serene and indeed attain that same merit.
By the power of this merit, they never go to an evil rebirth;
having always enjoyed auspicious happiness, they go to the abode of the Victors.
Therefore, those who desire the happiness of the true Dharma should always, with all effort and devotion,
observe the vow of day and night.
There is no measure to the merit produced by this vow of day and night.
"It is proclaimed by the Buddhas as immeasurable and incalculable."
Even by all the lords of sages, it is impossible to calculate its number;
how could I alone here possibly calculate that merit?
By the power of whose merit even great sins are utterly consumed, so that, with a purified self, one attains a happy rebirth at that very moment.
Having accomplished their desired task without obstacle,
and having always enjoyed sublime happiness, they finally go to the abode of the Victors.
Thinking thus, men should always practice this excellent vow of day and night, which yields great merit, for the attainment of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
If you do so, there will always be great merit and auspiciousness for you in this world and the next;
having gradually attained the vow of enlightenment, you will certainly become a bodhisattva.
Having gradually conquered the afflictions, you who delight in the pleasures of cyclic existence,
and having defeated all the hosts of Māra, may you attain the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having heard this very great merit thus explained by the wise Vasubandhu, Indra rejoiced at that which he had asked.
Then that great king, named Indrapṛṣṭha, being thus encouraged,
desired to observe and cause others to observe the vow of a single day and night.
Then that king, rising up with palms joined in reverence, approached Vasubandhu; bowing down before him, he made this request with great respect: Avc_55 //
"Venerable sir, having heard that great merit arising from the vow of day and night (ahorātravrata) taught by you, I now desire to perform it."
Therefore, you ought to instruct me in that method for the welfare of the world;
I shall practice it in every way, and so too will all living beings.
Therefore, for the benefit of all sentient beings and for the accomplishment of merit,
you should instruct us in the ritual procedure for this day-and-night vow.
Having heard this request made by that lord of men, the high-minded Vasubandhu spoke thus to him, as if questioned by Indra himself.
Listen, O King, to that which was proclaimed by the Lord of Sages, Vipaśyin;
I shall likewise explain to you the procedure for the King of Vows in its proper sequence.
At a self-arisen shrine or sacred ground, in a monastery or a hermitage of the Sugata, at a field of merit, on a riverbank, or likewise at the confluence of rivers; Avc_61 //
At a sacred ford, on the seashore, on the bank of a lake, at the edge of a pond,
in a garden, on a mountain, in a forest, in a secluded place, or in a forest hermitage.
In a shrine, a sacred place, a palace, a temple, or a house—
likewise in any other region on earth that is a pure and delightful location.
When these have been purified and the desired site has been cleansed,
one should first construct a Dharma-hall and smear it with clay and cow dung.
Having erected four banners, one should spread out a canopy;
one should decorate it with various flower garlands and the like, as well as with fine cloths and silk bands.
{E adds a verse in the margin as follows:
One should smear [the image] with cow’s milk, the five jewels, and powdered stone; [one should adorn it] with garlands of the directions and the splendors of the directions.}
And one should cause [the image] to hang in a temple of the Jina.
There, the Vajrin of auspicious conduct, whose three spheres (maṇḍala) are completely purified,
should construct a beautiful maṇḍala of the dharmadhātu according to the ritual rules.
Then the Vajrin, having established that mandala according to the ritual procedure and having gathered those observing the vows, should cause the commencement of the observance.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, at the end of the meal and at the close of the day,
having cleansed one's teeth and so forth, one should purify the mouth and other parts.
On the morning of the fourteenth day, having bathed at the sacred ford, the wise practitioner, clad in clean garments, of auspicious character, and endowed with faith, [should perform the rite].
At midday, having duly worshipped the maṇḍala and the caitya with the five offerings, one should perform prostration.
Then, during the third watch of the day, one should have the observance of the vow performed;
thereafter, one should have a bath performed with pure foods that are free from meat.
Then, at the beginning of the night, one should worship the shrine and the mandala;
having lit rows of lamps, one should cause the practitioners to hear the Dharma.
On the full moon day, having bathed at dawn and being clothed in clean garments,
they should perform the purification of their limbs with the purified five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then, having first offered the *argha* to the Sun, those observers of the vow likewise offered the *argha* to their preceptor, and each stood upon his own seat in due order.
And they should purify all the components of the worship according to the ritual rules;
there, at the outset, that assembly of practitioners should worship Vajrasattva.
Then one should worship the Three Jewels according to the ritual procedure;
having gone for refuge to them, one should prostrate with palms joined in reverence.
Then, having performed the threefold samādhi and meditated upon the Lord of Jinas within oneself,
one should invoke the glorious Maheśvara, the Dharmadhātu, before one.
Then one should offer the *argha* for his feet, followed by the *argha* for sipping water (*ācamana*).
Having then offered the *argha* for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), one should establish him within the mandala.
Then, having joyfully worshipped that maṇḍala together with its retinue using offerings of worship according to the ritual rules, the wise practitioner should recite the heart-mantra of that [deity].
{E adds here:
Then one should recite the hymn:
"The shrine consisting of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), whose very nature is all forms."}
I pay homage to the Lord of Speech, the abode of all Buddhas.
The entire realm born of the Victors has been made fruitful as a field of merit;
it is bestowed for the sake of the happiness of all people and for the purpose of being served.

Bow down to the King of Sages, who stands with palms joined in reverence, the preeminent one who has conquered all fear and its objects, the Lord of the World, the Great Master. Then, having recited this hymn of praise, one should satisfy him with hands joined in *añjali*.
One should perform the confession of misdeeds and likewise rejoice in merit.
Then one should perform circumambulations and hold a great festival with musical performances;
having performed prostrations with the eight limbs, one should pray for the vow of awakening (*bodhisaṃvara*).
Then, having made a request for forgiveness, one should dismiss that maṇḍala. (Avc 81)
Just as worship was performed there in the mandala according to the ritual, so too, having thoroughly honored the caitya and the image, one should pray with such devotion: Avc_82 //
Likewise, one should joyfully perform worship and other rites at all shrines;
one should thus hold a great festival with hymns accompanied by music.
Having performed circumambulations and abandoned the languor of sleep,
one should joyfully keep watch throughout the day and night and observe the vow.
Likewise, having bathed at the four junctions of the day, one should perform service to the *caityas*.
One of a wicked birth must not be touched; if one is touched, one should perform a bath.
The practitioner of the vow should never take rest, nor should he feel weariness in his mind;
intent upon the meditation on the Caitya and absorbed in samādhi, he should proceed while reciting and chanting hymns.
One should propagate the great festival with the great enthusiasm of dance and song, with various musical instruments accompanied by dancing, with shouts of "Hāhā! and exultations.
In this manner, one should observe the vow without rest for a full day and night;
then, having bathed in the morning, one should worship the maṇḍala and the caitya.
Then, with great festivities, one should cause the parasol, the banners, along with the vessel of vermilion, and the parched grain, unbroken rice, and flowers to be raised up.
The wielder of the thunderbolt should perform the sacrifice and offer the oblation according to the ritual rules;
then, having bestowed the consecration, he should proceed in sequence with the five-threaded pitcher.
The wielder of the vajra, being composed, should bestow blessings even upon those observing the vows.
Then, having made a request for forgiveness, he should dismiss that mandala.
Then all those practitioners, having honored their preceptor, the Vajrācārya, and the ascetics,
and having given them the ritual fee, should satisfy them by bowing down.
Then, having taken that water and worshipped the nāgas at the sacred bathing place (tīrtha),
he should cause it to be carried to his home from there amidst auspicious festivities.
There, one should consecrate that site of the maṇḍala with water from a sacred ford (tīrtha);
then all those observers of the vow should perform the observance of that vow.
Then, at the site of that maṇḍala, the Vajrācārya, having worshipped the maiden according to the ritual rules, should satisfy her—the goddess—with various foods. Avc_95 //
Then, having honored the gaṇacakra, one should fully satisfy it with foods;
one should also satisfy the practitioners observing vows, the adepts, and all people.
Those mortals who thus joyfully observe the vow of day and night become great beings, Bodhisattvas of pure intention.
They do not go to an evil rebirth, but always go to a happy destination;
having enjoyed the joy and vigor of the Dharma, they proceed to the abode of the Victors.
Thus was it proclaimed by the Teacher Vipaśyin, and heard by me;
listen further, O Great King, specifically to its fruits.
Those who here bathe the shrine of the Lord of Jinas with the five nectars and the five fragrant waters,
having bathed in the divine, fragrant waters of the Mandākinī, they rejoice eternally among the gods.

{B has the following additional verse here: "Those who offer argha at a caitya with the five nectars, the five fragrant jewels, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, flowers, parched grain, and water, obtain a great treasure in this world."}
Those people who create a water-maṇḍala at a caitya with well-ground fragrant powder become golden-hued, born into royal lineages, prosperous, and fortunate.

Those people who, with pure minds, offer fragrant incense before the shrines and images of the Jinas, causing them to rejoice, become human beings with fragrant bodies who are honored by the hosts of gods.

Those people who, with faith, anoint the stūpa of the Perfectly Awakened One with the five fragrances, will have bodies perfumed with scent and possess strength and radiance; they shall be born in the worlds of ultimate reality.
Those who offer a sacrificial thread dyed with excellent colors and beautiful robes at a caitya will have gentle bodies clothed in divine garments and become filled with the perfection of all goals.
Those who, having bowed down, worship the shrine with all kinds of flowers possessing excellent fragrances,
shall be free from disease, long-lived, fortunate, and of very extensive lineage.
And those who likewise adorn a shrine with garlands made of beautiful flowers, they become fortunate ones with their limbs adorned; they become renowned gods and kings.
Those who arrange garlands of lamps at a shrine become filled with treasures and a wealth of jewels;
they become beautiful to behold and pleasing to the eyes, their nets of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom.
{A has two additional verses here:} He who,
together with his attendants, conquered the enemy of Smara upon the adamantine seat (vajrāsana),
as well as the enemies that are the afflictions (kleśa) and the wicked ones who range within the realm of sense-objects; [he is the one who...]

The Sugata, though having forcibly overcome aversion even toward the aggregates and having conquered death, became like one destitute and powerless when he was offered milk-rice, despite his mastery over the enjoyment of all the finest flavors.
Whether made of gold, silver, various metals, or clay, a bowl filled to the brim with rice from the *śāli* paddy,
one gives with devotion to the image or the shrine within a Sugata’s temple.
Their merit shall be peerless, and its fruit immeasurable.

(Avc 107) And those who offer excellent, divine, and supreme food as an offering to a shrine or an image, they become the best in the world, endowed with power and fame—kings of renowned majesty. (Avc 108)
And those who, out of devotion, offer fruits, leaves, roots, trunks, and so forth at a shrine,
become free from disease, highly prosperous, possessed of all they desire, and happy.
Those people who, with serene faith, offer medicine at the stūpa of a Perfectly Awakened One,
become kings and lords with smooth faces, possessing a golden complexion and free from disease.
{B, which was noted above as differing from version ii, adds another verse: "The excellent buffalo milk, combined with ghee... }
Those who constantly give to that preeminent among Jinas attain sovereignty together with royal splendor.
Those who offer betel, areca nuts, and other elixirs before the image of a shrine become rulers of the earth, fortunate, and possessed of faces that captivate the eyes of celestial women.
{A and B have the following additional verse here:

"In the cities of the gods and asuras, that which was held by the lotus-petal hands of beloveds— resplendent with excellent color and fragrance, and pleasant to the touch and delicious— was [consumed] by the hosts of deities."}
They eat divine nectar placed in radiant golden vessels;
that is the fruit of having given gifts of food dedicated to the Noble Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
And those who hoist bright-colored, variegated banners upon a shrine or an image—
Those lords of the earth who have conquered the hosts of the wicked become blessed and renowned for their majesty.
Those people who, with serene faith, extend a vast canopy over the image of a caitya from afar, become lords of gods and lords of men; they are blessed and possess renowned supernatural powers.
And those people who hang various pure banners at a shrine shall be endowed with glory both in heaven and on earth, becoming lords esteemed by the thirty-three gods.

Those people who, with serene faith, place upon the image of a shrine a parasol made of gold, variegated with jewels, silk ribbons, and sprinkled with flowers, while accompanied by auspicious musical instruments— Avc_115.
Those guardians of the Dharma, endowed with auspicious renown, abodes of fortune, and possessed of glory, virtues, and happiness,
become sovereigns of gods and lords of men, delighting in the conduct of awakening.

And those who bestow a great festival at the shrine with songs and musical instruments of most charming sound, with the loud and auspicious clamor of conchs and the like, and with the lovely tones of lutes, flutes, and so forth; Avc_117 //
Possessing divine ears and most pleasing speech, endowed with beauty of form and pure minds,
they become lords of mortals and gods, always possessing great supernatural powers and being deeply devoted to the Sugata.

Those who with delight worship the image of the Caitya through beautiful dances and most charming expressions, become free from evil, malevolent planets, and diseases; they become meritorious and endowed with the goal of virtuous qualities.

Furthermore, those people who, even while warding off the wicked, constantly protect a shrine— those fortunate ones, free from disease and of noble lineage, having enjoyed happiness and sovereignty, will proceed to heaven.
And those who, having offered durvā grass, kunda flowers, unbroken rice, parched grain, and so forth, bow down to a caitya,
become masters of knowledge, possessed of great prosperity, and in the end go even to the abode of the Sugata.

Those humans who, with devotion and affection, offer pure jewels such as diamonds and pearls, as well as excellent substances like gold and the eight precious metals, to the images of the Caityas; Avc_122 //
With their faculties complete and their desires fulfilled, they are free from sorrow, fortunate, and of noble lineage;
devoted to virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and delighting in excellent qualities, they have entered the path of the Perfectly Awakened One.
Those people who, with pure minds and full of faith, worship the reliquary with well-sung hymns of praise,
become lords on earth and in heaven, possessing the desired success of virtue, wealth, and pleasure.
Those who, with faith and serene confidence, having gone for refuge, bow down to a shrine with the eight limbs,
become wise and successful kings endowed with the seven excellent jewels.
Those who, full of joy and serene, circumambulate and bow down before the image of a shrine and wander [in devotion],
become golden-hued, of most noble lineage, and worthy of honor even by kings.
Those who joyfully smear the stūpa with fragrant waters mixed with pure stone-ash become free from disease and grief, possessed of great prosperity, long-lived, and fortunate.
Those who cleanse the courtyard of a shrine, removing faded garlands and sweeping it clean,
become golden-hued, pure in mind, devoted to the Dharma, and possessors of excellent vision.
Even if one performs a circumambulation of a stūpa out of laziness,
one shall obtain the fruit of giving one *karṣa* of gold at every step.
The temple of the Jina should be worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings by Brahmins;
likewise, the lowering of the parasol over the caitya should be performed by Kṣatriyas as well.
The lowering of the banner, along with the flag, is the duty to be performed by the Vaiśyas;
however, the Śūdras must offer only the food-oblation (naivedya) to the most eminent Caitya.
A temple of the Victor (jinālaya) must not be worshipped by others of inferior caste;
it is not to be honored with incense, lamps, and so forth, nor otherwise.
Likewise, with roots, trunks, leaves, fruits, stalks, and grain, as well as with rice and other cereals, and with medicinal herbs and elixirs; Avc 133.
Likewise, the temple of the Jina should be honored with musical instruments, beautiful songs, dances, and great festivals, as well as with shouts of "Hāhā! and exultations.
Even by leather-workers, boatmen, barbarians, officials, hunters, and others,
the temple of the Jina must be circumambulated from a distance and saluted.
Thus, the abode of the Victor should be worshipped by all people in the world, including the twice-born and all other castes, with honors appropriate to their respective classes.
Those people who joyfully observe the vow of day and night in this manner,
being liberated from all evil, shall proceed to the abode of the Victors.
Thinking thus, O Great King, you ought always, month after month,
on the full moon day, to observe the vow of fasting for a day and night.
Especially in the month of Aśvinī, when the lunar disc is full,
on a Sunday conjoined with the asterism Aśvinī and the yoga Puṣya.
On an auspicious day of a great festival joined with this yoga,
one should, being composed, perform the vow for a full day and night according to the prescribed rule.
The man who performs the vow of day and night on that day shall certainly obtain merit a thousand times greater than that. Avc_141 //
Thus, O King, the merit of the vow of a single day and night is said by the Buddhas to be exceedingly great— immeasurable and incalculable.
For there is no one, O King, even throughout all the worlds,
who can otherwise produce the merit arising from the vow of day and night.
Merely by hearing it, one is liberated from all transgressions;
likewise, one obtains merit through seeing it and even through rejoicing in it.
O Great King, who indeed would be able to calculate the measure of the merit of those who likewise practice this king of vows? Avc_145 //
The king shall obtain one-seventh part of that merit;
likewise, all sentient beings shall obtain one part, and likewise, the practitioners shall obtain one part.
Indeed, all those who observe the vow obtain a fourth part of that merit;
through the power of this merit, there is always auspiciousness everywhere.
"May all sentient beings be rich in happiness and practice the conduct of awakening.
Having understood this, O King of Kings, as the means for accomplishing the welfare of the world,
you ought by all means to observe the vow of day and night."
Having heard this which was thus related by the wise Vasubandhu, Indrapṛṣṭha desired to perform that vow.
Then that illustrious king, the lord of men, being questioned by Indra,
bowed again with palms joined in reverence and made this request to Vasubandhu.
"O Venerable One, Omniscient Teacher, bearing your command upon my head,
I now truly desire to perform the vow of the day and night."
O Teacher, you who possess great wisdom and whose intention is the welfare of all sentient beings,
please grant me your permission for the sake of accomplishing the benefit and purpose of all.
Having heard this request made by that lord of men, the high-minded Vasubandhu spoke thus to the king: Avc_153 //
Excellent, excellent, Great King! If you so desire, then joyfully perform this great merit, the vow of day and night.
By doing that for them, great merit will arise, and there will be auspiciousness everywhere;
through the ripening of this merit, one may even attain perfect enlightenment.
Having heard what was thus instructed by the Teacher, that king, being questioned by Indra, bowed with palms joined and spoke again in this manner: Avc_156 //
"Venerable Sir, I wish to build a temple for the Victor in a field of merit;
you should deign to point out which field is the most meritorious. (1151)
When the king had thus questioned him, that wise omniscient Vasubandhu instructed the monarch once again in this way: Avc_158 //
Listen, O virtuous great king, to how it has been proclaimed by the lords of sages; I shall explain it to you just so, and having heard it, you ought to act accordingly.
Vārāṇasī is renowned as the greatest of all lands;
it is a field of merit, a great seat (mahāpīṭha), praised by all the Buddhas.
In that regard, whatever action has been performed through a formal vow succeeds exactly so both in this life and in the next, and certainly not otherwise.
Having understood this, O Indra among kings, go there and,
having duly established a caitya, observe the vow for a day and a night.
If you act thus, prosperity will surely be yours always, both in this world and the next;
having gradually fulfilled the practices of awakening, you shall attain the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard this instruction given by his preceptor Vasubandhu,
that illustrious king agreed, saying, "So be it."
Then, having been questioned by Indra and placing his teacher Vasubandhu before him,
he returned and approached Vārāṇasī.
Having arrived there, that lord of the earth, having inspected the auspicious ground,
first performed the purification of the site and examined the Vāstu-nāga.
Having duly constructed a monastery as well as a stūpa and a temple for the Jina,
and having consecrated the Three Jewels according to the ritual, he always paid them homage.
Thereupon, that king of men began to observe that vow exactly as it had been instructed by his teacher, Vasubandhu.
Then, having formally taken up the vow together with his wife, that lord of kings observed the one-day-and-night fast and worshipped that stūpa according to the prescribed rite.
Having completed that, he again invited Dīpaṃkara along with his community of monks there and honored them with food as was appropriate.
Then that protector of the earth, having devotedly served that caitya for a long time and having enjoyed true happiness, finally departed for the abode of the Jina.
Thus, this great merit arising from the vow of a single day and night is declared by all the Buddhas to be immeasurable and incalculable.
In the same way, you too should always observe the vow for that day and night here,
and having worshipped the reliquary, you should serve it with constant reverence.
In this way, may there be constant and certain auspiciousness for you here and in the hereafter;
having attained awakening in due course, you shall reach the state of final liberation.
Having heard what was thus commanded by the Lord of Sages, those monks joyfully consented,
saying "So be it," and desired to undertake that vow.
Then those monks, having bowed with palms joined in reverence to their Teacher, the Lord of Sages, questioned him thus with great devotion.
O Blessed One, we have heard all that was performed as instructed by you when questioned by Indra; we wish to hear it once again.
By whom and in what manner was this supreme vow previously performed?
It behoves you to instruct us regarding that great merit of a single day and night.
When he had been asked thus by those monks, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages, looked upon all those monks belonging to the Saṅgha and spoke as follows: Avc_179 //
Listen, all you monks, and others as well, to what was done in the past;
I shall relate it all for your enlightenment.
Formerly, in heaven, Indra likewise established a temple for the Jina;
having observed the vow of fasting for a day and night, he worshipped the shrine according to the prescribed rite.
By the power of this merit, that wise Mahāsattva, having gradually fulfilled all the perfections, became a Bodhisattva.
{E adds: Then, at another time, there was another king of the gods;
having enjoyed the pleasures of the king of the gods, he roamed about here according to his desire.}
And in the netherworld (pātāla), there was a great hero, a lord of the Daityas possessed of mighty supernatural power (maharddhimat),
named Nirghoṣadamana, who struck fear into the world of the gods.
Having conquered even the three worlds by that power, he brought them under his own control;
and having defeated all the world-protectors as well, he brought them under his control.
Then, having gone to the earth, he approached Vārāṇasī;
seeing the caitya situated at Indrapṛṣṭhavihāra, he rejoiced.
Then, having circumambulated that shrine according to the prescribed rite and worshipped it, he joined his palms in reverence and, bowing low, made this request: Avc_186 //
Having enjoyed happiness for as long as life lasts and having brought the world under my own control,
may I go for refuge to the Perfectly Awakened One and, at the end, proceed to the abode of the Victor.
Having thus made this vow and bowed to that abode of the Jina,
the lord of the Daityas, possessed of great supernatural power, departed from that very place for heaven.
And there, having beheld the shrine established by Śakra in ancient times, he bowed down,
circumambulated it, and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite.
Having made such a vow and bowed with joy and palms joined,
he then returned and went to his own home in Pātāla.
By the power of this merit, that lord of the Daityas, possessed of great supernatural might, then obtained the throne of Śakra there along with his hosts and forces. (Avc_190*)
Then the lord of the gods, having perceived that Aho had arrived, thought:
"Now, by what means shall I conquer this Dānava?
He who was named Damana resides in my hermitages. (Avc 190)
Having reflected thus, Śakra established a caitya in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven for the sake of worship by the former lords of the gods. Avc_190***
At that caitya, I shall observe the vow for a day and night according to the prescribed rule;
by that means and through righteousness, I shall conquer the enemy of the gods.
I have heard that there is the True Dharma; therefore, he too, by means of those vows and accompanied by the gods, has gone to heaven, to the realm of Maghavan.
And immediately thereafter, the Lord of Gods performed the worship of the vows with highly precious offerings and an exceedingly magnificent assembly in the temple of the Jina.
Immediately thereafter, Nirghoṣadama, having been defeated by the asuras,
was brought down to earth after conquering the asura without a battle.
There, that lord of the Daityas [constructed] a temple for the Jina according to the prescribed rite.
Having established a great reliquary, he honored it and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite.
Then that lord of the Daityas, having undertaken the vow for a day and night according to the prescribed rite, honored that shrine.
Having made such a vow there, that great-minded lord of the asuras always worshipped him according to the prescribed rites and constantly honored him with great festivals.
Having thus enjoyed great happiness for as long as he lived,
he took refuge in that caitya and likewise went to the abode of the Jina.
Likewise, other nāga kings also resorted to that caitya,
and having undertaken the vow of day and night, they honored it and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite.
In that way, all those nāgas, having enjoyed great happiness for as long as they lived through the power of their merit, went at the end to the abode of the Jina.
Likewise, in the land of Magadha, there was a great lake within a sacred shrine,
filled with pure water and beautifully adorned with lotuses, water lilies, and other such flowers.
There, in the temple of the Jina situated in the middle of the lake, the sages,
having undertaken the vow of fasting for a day and night, honored it and worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
Thus was the shrine worshipped by those sages while they remained at that lake.
Upon seeing him, eight Naga maidens approached his presence.
There, those seers, struck by the poisonous breaths of those [nāgas] and rendered doubtful by the poison, fainted for a mere moment.
Then all those sages, having regained their consciousness in an instant and seeing those Naga maidens sitting together, cursed them in anger.
"You are wicked and most sinful, since we have been tormented by the fires of your poison; therefore, by your own demerits, may you become śambuka fish!"
Thus sworn by all those sages, they were filled with fear; bowing down to all the best of sages, they entreated them thus with reverence: Avc_203 //
Homage be to you, O possessors of great wisdom! Forgive our transgressions;
you ought to instruct us in the means for liberation from that curse.
Having heard this request made by them, those great seers, their hearts overcome with compassion upon beholding them, spoke as follows: Avc_205 //
"Listen, you Śambukas! Hear this means for liberation from the curse taught by us, and practice it with reverence."
Taking the image of the shrine as an object of focus and recollecting it with the mind,
one should always perform circumambulation, moving around it and honoring it with devotion.
Then, by the power of that merit, being liberated from all evils,
you sons of kings will become auspicious ones with purified intentions.
For even then, you, being thus devoted to the service of the caityas and having accomplished the practice of the True Dharma, shall go to the abode of the Victors.
Having heard this truthful instruction given by those sages,
the Śambukas bowed to the sages and then departed for their own abodes.
Then all those śambukas approached the rice field;
recollecting the image of the shrine, they wandered about on every side.
There, having beheld the stalk of rice with its remaining parts severed,
they took it as the form of a shrine and recollected the abode of the Sugata.
Having always circumambulated [the stūpas] and bowed down again and again,
and having maintained the recollection of the Caityas, they wandered about and then departed.
There, all those Śambukas, purified by his merit,
set out in haste, mindful of the stūpa, for the sake of being released from his curse.
Once, a fisherman of cruel mind, seeking fish, approached that lake to catch the fish dwelling therein. Avc_215 //
There, that fisherman, eager to catch fish,
stood on the shore, cast out his net, and set about gathering them.
When that net was cast, by the turn of fate all the *śambuka* fish entered it, but not a single *matsya* at all.
Then, having pulled out his net and spread it out to examine it, he saw only shells there; not a single fish was to be found.
Then, failing to catch the fish, he took those very *śambuka* shells and,
his spirit exhausted, slowly returned to his own home.
Having arrived at his own home there, dejected and hopeless,
he presented those shells before his wife, Sundarikā.
Then that fisherman, intent on catching fish elsewhere, took whatever food he had obtained, ate it, and set out taking his net. Avc_221 //
Then that fisherwoman, seeing those śambūka shells placed before her and observing them as she was hungry, sighed and spoke thus: Avc_222 //
"Alas, what a tragedy! What shall I do today? There is no food at all in my house. Who would buy these oyster shells? How indeed shall I survive here? (Avc 223)
"Therefore, having cooked all these snails here now, I shall eat them;
by this food alone I shall sustain myself, and not otherwise."
Having thus resolved, that woman, seeking to save her life, cooked all those śambūkas herself with spices and ate them.
Then, by the turn of fate, all those śambukas entered her very womb and became merged into a single mass.
Then she became pregnant; bearing her advanced pregnancy, day by day her limbs grew heavy, she took pleasure in eating little, and she became emaciated.
Then, in due time, she gave birth to eight beautiful daughters,
born from a single womb, identical in form and endowed with auspicious qualities.
There, having seen those eight beautiful infants,
who were identical in form and possessed of lovely limbs, that mother was filled with wonder as she gazed upon them.
Then Janaka, having heard that eight sons had indeed been born, was struck with wonder; approaching suddenly, he stood gazing, utterly motionless.
Then all those girls, protected by their mother,
grew up with well-nourished limbs and shone like lotuses.
Then all those maidens, empowered by the majesty of their former merit,
awakened to love and confidence, and possessed intentions delighted in the Dharma and its purpose.
Terrified for their own families' livelihoods, yet moist with compassion and filled with pity,
they proceeded forth, endowed with the zeal to behold the Three Jewels.
Then her mother summoned all those girls as well and sent them to the marketplace for the purpose of selling fish.
Then, taking all those fish-trays, all those girls set out along the streets of that city to sell them.
Having proceeded there in succession, they all rested for a moment on the bank of a river not far from the path, and upon seeing it, they took refuge right there.
Among them, the eldest sister was the wise Sudhī;
seeing all those sisters, she addressed them and spoke as follows. Avc_237 //
"Sisters, because of the terrible sin we committed in the past, we have now been born here in the family of a caṇḍāla. (Avc 238)
Having thus fully understood this truth and desisted from evil deeds,
we ought always to delight in accomplishing the goals of Dharma.
If we were to perform such means for accomplishing evil here as well,
we would again fall into hell and wander about after experiencing suffering.
When shall we be liberated from that, and how shall we find happiness?
For we are always born in miserable states and thus continue to practice only in evil deeds.
Without merits, one will never again obtain birth in the human state;
and when the human state is not obtained, where could one direct the mind toward the Dharma?
O auspicious one, how could one venture to practice without the mind of Dharma?
Without the *Bhadracaryā*, how could one attain a good rebirth in the world?
And even in a happy rebirth, one will never obtain happiness without the dharmas;
therefore, fixing the mind upon the Dharma, one should always practice what is wholesome.
Through virtue they have gone to a good rebirth; through evil they have gone to a miserable rebirth.
Having experienced pleasure and pain, sentient beings wander in existence. Therefore, in order to attain a good rebirth from here, let us always practice virtue.
Moreover, since we are all born of the Caṇḍāla caste, how could we abandon our family livelihood, O auspicious lady? (Avc 246)
Since we were indeed commissioned by our mother to sell fish, how could we possibly act otherwise, disregarding our mother’s words? (Avc 247)
If we do not sell these here and cast them into the reservoir, how can we go before our mother at home with empty hands? (Avc 248)
"That which we lack for our enjoyment at home—this indeed is life itself.
How then could that mother eat, for she cannot live without food?"
Therefore, what shall we do here? Fie upon our birth, even though it be human! Better is the abandonment of life than the accomplishment of sinful purposes.
Since death is inevitable for all living beings, realizing this, we should always abide in what is virtuous within this saṃsāra. (Avc 251)
Therefore, in this matter, let us throw these living fish into a body of water,
sell them only after they have died, and give the proceeds to our mother.
If this is done by us in such a way, no sin indeed exists for us; rather, some merit would exist. Therefore, we shall act accordingly.
Having heard these words of mine in this matter, you should consent to act accordingly;
indeed, we ought not to cause you any distress or despair.
Having heard what was thus related by her, they were awakened;
and having agreed, saying "So be it," they desired to emulate her.
Then all those maidens, having suddenly seized all those fish that were still alive, threw them into the waters of that river.
Taking all those whose life-breaths had departed,
they went to the city and sold them as was appropriate.
Then, taking that wager, all those maidens returned home with joy and presented the entire proceeds to their mother.
Thus urged by their mother, those maidens likewise threw the living ones into the water and took a wager with the lifeless ones.
Thus, having always and constantly performed those acts, and having eaten and been entertained, they became terrified by that mode of livelihood; fearing sin, they despaired.
On a certain day, all those mothers were urged in that manner; taking fish to sell, they went together to the marketplace. Avc_261 //
There, by a stroke of fate, all those fish were restored to life;
seeing them all alive, they all were filled with wonder.
There, having looked at one another, all those maidens stood still after saying, "How shall we act here today? (Avc 263)
There, that chief among them—a girl of pure intention and wise mind—seeing all those sisters and consoling them, spoke thus: (Avc 264)
"Sisters, since all these fish are indeed living beings,
how can we now sell them here even though they are alive?"
Therefore, having cast all these fish here into the waters of the river,
remain here for one day while recollecting the Three Jewels.
If we go home empty-handed without any money,
our mother will surely become angry, cry out in distress, and beat us all.
Furthermore, if there is no food whatsoever to be found anywhere in the house today, how could a mother eat her own food while she wanders about hungry and filled with anger? (Avc 268)
And what would he give us, even food and drink, if he were provoked to anger? Having rebuked us repeatedly, he might even have the fools expelled from the house. (Avc 269)
Therefore, why go home today? Let us all gather here together and remain until the end of the day, recollecting the Three Jewels.
Having heard what she had said, all those maidens also agreed,
saying "So be it," and threw all the fish into the water.
There, all those maidens, having taken refuge on the banks of the river,
remained composed in meditation after recollecting the Three Jewels.
Having heard from someone else this account of their conduct,
her mother, scorched by the fire of anger, went there in haste with fury.
There, having seen all those girls standing in that manner, their mother suddenly approached, rebuked them, and spoke as follows: (Avc 274)
"O unfortunate children, why do you remain here in this manner? Even at nightfall, for what reason have you not come home? (Avc 275)
"Why do you release all these fish without selling them?
There is no food at all in the house; so what shall we eat now?"
Tell me this: having heard whose instruction do you disregard the duties of your family, and ignoring even the words of your parents, do you thus indulge in play? Avc_277
When this was said by her mother, all those maidens also remained with their faces cast down; overcome with despondency, they did not say anything at all.
Seeing her daughters standing there in that manner, their mother, overcome with rage,
suddenly approached them and struck them with a club.
Then that mother, seeing them all with terrified faces,
diligently awakened them and led them to her own home at night.
There, all those maidens, remaining in their own home at night,
stood in a secluded spot without eating, recollecting the Lord of Sages.
And on the following day, that mother, having killed live fish and given them to those girls, sent them into the city for sale.
Realizing that their mother had acted in such a way, all those maidens also reflected upon that evil deed and remained there, distressed by the sin.
Seeing them all standing there in that manner, their mother, filled with rage,
rebuked them many times, struck them, and drove them out of the city.
Then all those girls, afflicted by the pain of that beating and despondent,
took those fish and went out slowly to sell them.
Then they all emerged and, on the bank of the lake by that path,
afflicted by the pain of being struck by their mother, rested for a moment and took refuge there.
There, all those maidens, in order to purify themselves of that sin,
remained absorbed in meditation after recollecting the Three Jewels.
Purified by that merit, they each constructed a stūpa with those sands, honoring it, installing it, and rejoicing.
There, having gathered the flowers and fruits that had grown on all sides,
they honored their respective *caityas* with those fruits and flowers.
Then, having joined their palms in reverence, performed circumambulations,
and prostrated with the eight limbs, they stood absorbed in meditative concentration.

"Master, all those girls have not yet returned home even now.
Go quickly to see where they have gone and bring them back."
Having heard this spoken by his wife, that Caṇḍāla was provoked to anger;
walking suddenly toward the shore of that lake, he saw them all.
There, seeing them all standing after having worshipped the shrine,
their father, consumed by extreme anger, suddenly came forward to face them.
There, upon seeing him approaching face-to-face with eyes red and burning with anger, all those maidens remained absorbed in meditative concentration.
Seeing all his own daughters standing there in that manner, he,
being merciless, rebuked them in many ways and even struck them with a club.
Likewise, though they were all beaten severely, they did not move;
terrified by that sin, they remained as if absorbed in meditative concentration.
Then that cruel Janaka, having beaten and reviled them,
suddenly took all those fish and wandered through his city.
There, having sold those fish and taken the food, he went quickly before his wife at home and reported that deed to her. (Avc 299)
There, afflicted by the unbearable pain arising from that beating,
they all rolled upon the ground, weeping, and remained unconscious.
Seated on the slope of the mountain near him, the Pratyekabuddha, a treasury of compassion and knower of the self, heard her lamentation.
There, looking all around with a compassionate gaze, he beheld them all, overcome by suffering and fallen into a swoon.
Then that skillful Pratyekabuddha, impelled by compassion,
suddenly approached that place and stood there, emitting moonlight.
Touched by those rays of nectar, they were all endowed with happiness;
having regained their consciousness, they all beheld that Lord of Ascetics.
Then, upon seeing that sage, their minds overcome with wonder,
they all stood there filled with joy, reflecting, "Who is this sage?"
Then their eldest sister, Vicakṣaṇā, seeing all those sisters, addressed them and spoke thus: Avc_306 //
We are truly fortunate today that this Sage of the Sugatas has come here in person out of compassion to deliver us.
If this Buddha Sudhāraśmi, the treasury of compassion, has not arrived,
we shall all perish right here, left without protection.
Blessed is this Sugata, the Protector who has compassion for all sentient beings;
for who else in the world of the three realms is a bringer of benefit besides the Buddha?
The Buddha alone is the teacher of the world, the accomplisher of all auspicious purposes,
the protector who rescues from miserable rebirths, and the guide who shows the path to the happy realms.
Therefore, we have all gone for refuge to him at all times;
let us honor him with faith and devotion, and serve him according to our ability.
Then, surely we shall all be liberated from every evil;
with our three bodies completely purified, we shall indeed go to a happy rebirth.
Having heard what she related,
they were all awakened and likewise desired to venerate that sage.
Then all those maidens, endowed with faith and devotion,
joyfully honored that sage with hospitable offerings according to their ability.
Then, having gone for refuge with hands joined in reverence, they joyfully circumambulated him three times, bowed down, and made this request: Avc_315 //
O Blessed One, O Protector, O Omniscient One, we always remain in refuge to you; we wish to practice exactly as you have instructed.
Therefore, beholding us who are so deeply distressed with your compassionate gaze,
you ought at all times to protect us and all others in that same way.
No other protector, lord, friend, well-wisher, or teacher exists for us;
you alone are our teacher, instructor, master of the true Dharma, and sovereign.
Therefore, beholding us all who are suffering with a compassionate gaze,
he ought to protect us by always establishing us on the path to enlightenment.
Having heard this request made by them, that Arhat of great intelligence,
a Pratyekabuddha Sugata, understood the ripening of their karma.
Then, leaping up into the sky and remaining there, blazing like a fire,
he displayed a miraculous feat for the purpose of gladdening that mind.
Having seen this miracle of his, they were all filled with wonder;
their lotus-like faces became beautifully serene, and their minds attained a state of well-acquired awakening.
There, having circumambulated [the Buddha] with joy and palms joined in reverence,
they prostrated themselves with the eight limbs and made the vow for enlightenment.
Through the ripening of this merit from the joyful honor we have rendered to this Sage, may we obtain birth in a happy state of existence.
Having accomplished the welfare of ourselves and others, and having performed virtuous deeds everywhere,
may we attain such a pratyekabuddha enlightenment and proceed to nirvāṇa.
Thus all those maidens, having made their vow and being filled with serene faith,
bowed to that very Sugata and stood absorbed in meditative concentration.
Having perceived that their hearts were thus transformed, the Sugata then suddenly approached from the sky and instructed them in this way: Avc_327 //
"Sisters, be well-pleased; for on the seventh day from now, you shall all, being of auspicious nature, pass away at the same time."
Then, having obtained birth in a royal family in Vārāṇasī, you who possess auspicious portions [of karma] shall all conduct yourselves properly and practice what is virtuous.
There, having observed that cyclic existence is crowded with afflictions,
you shall abandon all possessions and delight in the forest of asceticism.
And there too, by always remaining composed through mindfulness of the Three Jewels,
you shall attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha and reach the state of nirvāṇa.
Having understood this, all of you sisters here, being composed,
should practice the worship of the Three Jewels and always conduct yourselves in what is auspicious.
Having thus instructed him, that Pratyekabuddha,
illuminating the sky, leaped up and suddenly departed for his own hermitage.
Seeing him situated in the sky, all those maidens, filled with joy and deeply inspired by faith, bowed down and after a long time returned to their own abodes.
Having worshipped that shrine there, they died on the seventh day;
they were reborn as the daughters of King Kṛka in Vārāṇasī, equal in status to the gods.
Of them, the eldest sister was known as Vratī;
the second was renowned as Dharmavatī; and the third was Śubhamañjarī.
The fourth is named Dhīmatī, the fifth is Netramañjarī;
the sixth is known as Śrīmatī, and the seventh is Madaṃjahā.
The eighth is named Ratnamālā; these are the eight maidens, the daughters of King Sujāta, who were of similar conduct and similar disposition.
Thereupon, those seven maidens, Dharmavatī and the others, who practice virtue,
beholding saṃsāra to be agitated by the afflictions, [abandoned] their possessions.
Having abandoned all their respective [possessions], they all went to the forest of asceticism.
And there too, always mindful of the Three Jewels and remaining composed,
they attained individual enlightenment and reached final liberation.
Among them, the eldest sister was she who practiced that vow throughout every birth;
by the power of this merit, that maiden became like Rati herself.
In the excellent city of Dharmapattana lived one named Vratī, whose character was devoted to Dharma;
she was the eldest and most eminent among them, a maiden like Rati herself,
who became the wife of King Dharmadakṣa and practiced the path of righteousness.
Even then, that maiden remained observant of her vows, devoted to the service of the *caityas*,
longing for the practice of awakening, and contemplating the qualities of the Perfectly Awakened One.
There, that virtuous maiden, desiring joyfully to perform the worship of the shrine, bowed to her husband, who was skilled in dharma, and requested him thus with reverence: Avc_341 //
"O Lord, I wish to perform the worship of the images in the caityas at all times, as well as the day-and-night vow; therefore, grant me your permission. (Avc 342)
Having heard this request joyfully made by his virtuous wife, and having looked upon her, the king spoke to his wife as follows: Avc_343 //
"O noble lady, it is well; you have rightly awakened me. I too shall practice the excellent vow day and night."
Having spoken thus, that king, skilled in dharma and filled with joy,
together with his wife, desired to undertake that excellent vow of day and night.
Then that king, having established the shrine according to the ritual rules and having observed the vow for a day and night, worshipped it together with his wife.
Thus, together with his virtuous wife Subhāvinī,
that king Dharmadakṣa was constantly devoted to the service of the caityas.
Then that couple, having performed worship of the Jina for as long as they lived and having enjoyed happiness, finally entered the abode of the Jina.
Thinking thus, you all should joyfully and with faith observe the noble vow here;
having undertaken the day-and-night vow, venerate the shrine with reverence.
For if you act in this way, there will always be welfare for you in this world and the next;
having gradually attained the state of enlightenment, you shall go to the abode of the Victors.
Having heard this instruction given by the Lord of Munis in the scripture,
those monks likewise undertook the vow and entered the sanctuary.
Thus it was told to me by my teacher, and thus have I heard it, O lord of men;
for the sake of the welfare of all the world, it is now being declared to you as well.
In the same way, O Great King, for the sake of attaining the state of perfect enlightenment,
observe the vow of day and night and be devoted to the service of the caityas.
By the power of this merit, may you have auspiciousness everywhere;
having always enjoyed true happiness, may you go at last to the abode of the Victors.
Furthermore, O Great King,
without the Dharma there is no liberation, and without giving there is no enjoyment.
Without hearing, true knowledge does not arise; therefore, practice the Dharma and other virtues.
"Indeed, the evil committed over seven lifetimes is destroyed by that very [practice];
furthermore, birth in a bad field or a low lineage shall no longer occur.
Having heard this teaching proclaimed by Upagupta, he...
Aśoka, together with the world of living beings, joyfully accepted this, saying, "So be it."
Those who, with pure minds, hear or cause others to hear this majesty of serving the caityas as taught by the Supreme Victor— listening with joyful hearts and being well-disposed through faith—
they shall be liberated from all afflictions, delight in the qualities of the Victor, and attain the mind of awakening.
Those of pure self and firm wisdom, who bring about all that is auspicious, proceed to the world of the Buddhas.
Thus ends the Avadāna on the Merit of Observing the Vow for a Day and Night and Serving a Caitya.
The *Śvadāna-aśokapṛcchita* is completed. May there be auspiciousness for the worlds. Written by Paṇḍita Mudā in the year 32, in the month of Āśvina, during the dark fortnight. E.
